vignette:
She has been coming to therapy for six weeks. She is twenty-three, South Asian, and works as an auditor for a mid-sized firm. She lives alone in a quiet apartment complex, miles from the neighborhood where her family's grocery store used to be. She does not talk about that neighborhood unless I ask. Even then, her sentences break off like branches under too much snow.

The trauma happened two years ago, during the last sustained offensive in her home city. She remembers the date because it was her brother's birthday. They were having a small celebration in the back room of the store-her mother had made gulab jamun, and her father was telling a story about the time he had to smuggle canned milk across a checkpoint. Then the air changed. She does not mean the sound. She means the pressure, the way the air compressed and then ripped apart. She describes it as a feeling like being unmade.

She was thrown against a shelf. Cans of chickpeas and tomatoes rained down on her. When she opened her eyes, she could not see her mother. The ceiling had collapsed. She heard her father calling her name from somewhere far away because his voice was coming through dust. She crawled toward it. She did not find her father. She found his arm, still attached to his body, but the rest of him was gone in a way she cannot describe. She does not try. She presses her palms to her eyes when she tells me this, as if she is still trying not to see.

Her brother survived, badly burned. Her mother was pulled from the rubble with a shattered pelvis. They left the city three days later, walking through checkpoints with no shoes, because the glass was everywhere and her shoes were somewhere in the wreckage. She does not remember the walk. She has no memory of anything from that moment until she was on a bus, staring at a woman's braid with a pink clip in it. That memory is crystal clear. The braid. The clip. She can draw it.

She came to this country on a humanitarian visa. She finished her degree in accounting because numbers felt safe. Addition and subtraction do not vary. They do not explode. She tells me she became an auditor because she likes that the rules are written down, and if she follows them, the answer is always the same. But lately, the numbers have started to feel like dust. She will be reviewing a balance sheet and suddenly she is back in the store, smelling kaolin and blood. The rows of figures blur into the rows of cans on the shelf. She blinks and it passes, but her heart is racing and she has to excuse herself to the restroom three times in a morning. Her supervisor has noticed. She has used all her sick days.

She avoids the break room because someone microwaved fish last week and the smell reminded her of the market near the bus station. She avoids the news. She avoids the comment section of any article about the conflict. She avoids staying up late because she knows the dreams will come, so she sleeps at 9 p.m. but wakes at 2 a.m., certain that she heard a mortar. She checks the window. She checks the door. She checks that her brother is still alive by texting him, even though it is 3 a.m. where he lives, and he does not reply until morning, and those hours of waiting are the worst.

She does not cry during our sessions. She sits very still, like an animal that has learned stillness is survival. Her hands are folded in her lap. Her voice is even. She says she does not feel anything most of the time, and then suddenly, without warning, she feels everything-a tidal wave that drowns her for an hour and leaves her curled on the bathroom floor, wondering why she is crying over a plumber's commercial.

She told me last week that she cannot remember what her father's laugh sounded like. She used to know. She says the memory is gone, replaced by the arm. She says she hates herself for that. She says she is not sure she deserves to be here, in a safe apartment, with a job that pays, while her brother still walks with a limp and her mother cannot climb stairs. She says these things without anger. She says them like they are facts in a ledger.

She is not sure why she keeps coming to see me. She says maybe she is just tired. But she comes. She sits. She tells me about the braid.
